newsitem.title: POLAND: US points to agriculture problems of EU growth.
newsitem.headline: US points to agriculture problems of EU growth.

text.p: The United States supports EU membership for Central and East European (CEE) states but wants to safeguard its own farm exports, a U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) official said in Warsaw on Tuesday.
Mary Lisa Madell, of the USDA Economic Research Service, also cautioned CEE countries over potential effects of the EU's unreformed Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) on their sectors.
Madell told an agriculture conference that U.S. trade relations with CEE states would be strengthened in general by their membership of the EU, but complicated in the farm sector.
"When Poland and other CEEs join the European Union, the U.S. will want to make sure its agricultural exports are not displaced," she said.
She said U.S. farm exports to CEE countries totalled $439 million in 1996, with $232 million to Poland, but these were strongly affected by crop developments in the region.

In 1996 U.S. grain and feed exports to the region reached $195 million in 1996, up from $86 million in 1995 because of poor harvests, but signs this year were that grain supplies were better and U.S. exports would consequently fall.
The U.S. was keen to expand high-value exports such as poultry meat, and hoped these would grow reflecting higher CEE incomes in the period before new members joined the EU.
The U.S., as with past EU accessions, will try to ensure through the World Trade Organisation that it is compensated for losses such exports may sustain once CEE countries join.

Madell said EU enlargement could create new markets for some U.S. products in the CEE, such as feedstuffs for growing meat production, but exports to the EU of such items as meat and dairy products, some fruit and vegetables could be displaced by CEE products after accession.
She added that the CAP, if applied to CEE countries, would bring higher production of grains, meat and dairy produce, adding to EU surpluses for exports on world markets.
"The U.S. is therefore concerned about the effects even greater surpluses might have on its exports to third countries," she said.

On the other hand, she said enlargement might spur the EU to farm sector reform because increased production under the CAP would be costly and make it hard for the Union to meet General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) commitments.
Madell said the CAP looked good for existing members.

"But, as a potential beneficiary, Poland and other CEEs should not assume that the CAP will necessarily benefit their agricultural sectors," she said, adding that the current policy distorted market forces and could hamper farm sector restructuring, especially by imposing production controls.

She warned CEEs that current EU members might protect their own farmers by setting production controls for new entrants at current production levels which have still not recovered after falling at the start of economic transitions.
"The production control measures might be set at a level lower than would result after completing the transition," she said.

Several CEE states are hoping they can begin accession talks early next year after the EU's current summit in Amsterdam clears the way. Hungary, Poland, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Slovenia, Estonia, Lithuania, Latvia, Bulgaria and Romania have applied for membership. Cyprus also hopes to join.
